title: High-Resolution DKIST/ViSP Observation Reveals Small-scale Photospheric Magnetic Flux beneath a Coronal Hole Region
summary: The magnetic unipolarity of photospheric regions beneath coronal holes is well established at spatial resolutions of about 1 arcsecond, but the effect of smaller-scale magnetic structures remains uncertain. We compare co-aligned observations from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) aboard the Solar Dynamics Observatory and the Visible Spectro-Polarimeter (ViSP) at the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST). HMI observes the Fe I 6173 Å line, while ViSP observes the Fe I 6302.5 Å line; both form at similar photospheric heights. We derive the line-of-sight magnetic field (B_LOS) from ViSP spectropolarimetric data using a Milne-Eddington inversion and compare it with the HMI field derived from vector magnetograms over a common coronal-hole region. ViSP detects smaller magnetic structures with stronger fields than HMI. The absolute mean field and mean absolute field are higher by factors of 1.30 and 1.37, respectively. HMI measures approximately 28% less unsigned magnetic flux and 24% less net signed magnetic flux than ViSP. A comparison of spatially degraded ViSP data with HMI indicates that differences in effective resolution and associated spatial averaging contribute to these discrepancies. Nevertheless, the magnetic flux imbalance remains similar: 69% for HMI and 65% for ViSP. Thus, the additional small-scale flux detected by ViSP does not substantially change the measured unipolarity in this region. Because ViSP has a limited field of view, observations covering entire coronal holes are needed to test whether this result holds more generally.

AI.tldr: DKIST/ViSP resolves smaller-scale photospheric magnetic structures under a coronal hole than SDO/HMI, measuring ~28% more unsigned and ~24% more net flux, but the unipolarity (flux imbalance) stays essentially unchanged (~65% vs ~69%).
AI.motivation: The magnetic unipolarity of photospheric regions beneath coronal holes is established only at ~1 arcsecond resolution; whether finer-scale magnetic structures alter the measured unipolarity and flux budget remains uncertain.
AI.method: Co-aligned HMI (Fe I 6173 Å) and DKIST ViSP (Fe I 6302.5 Å) observations of a common coronal-hole region at similar photospheric heights. Line-of-sight field (B_LOS) from ViSP spectropolarimetry via Milne-Eddington inversion, compared with HMI vector-magnetogram-derived field; spatially degraded ViSP data compared against HMI to isolate resolution/averaging effects.
AI.result: ViSP detects smaller structures with stronger fields; absolute mean field and mean absolute field are higher by factors of 1.30 and 1.37. HMI measures ~28% less unsigned flux and ~24% less net signed flux than ViSP. Degraded ViSP comparison indicates differences in effective resolution and spatial averaging drive the discrepancies. Magnetic flux imbalance is similar: 69% (HMI) vs 65% (ViSP).
AI.conclusion: Additional small-scale flux detected by ViSP does not substantially change the measured unipolarity in this region. Because ViSP has a limited field of view, full-coronal-hole observations are needed to test generality.

title: The Stability Frontier of Interacting Binary Stars
summary: We derive a conservation based dynamical stability frontier for interacting binary stars that distinguishes stationary mass transfer from the restoration of a perturbed contact state. We apply the formalism to conservative white dwarf binaries with direct impact accretion, coupling Roche overflow, stream angular momentum, gravitational radiation, and both stellar spin reservoirs. From the contact equations, we obtain the required orbital return torque, and an exact Jacobian identity yields the restoring gradient and an oscillatory stability boundary in the computed white dwarf domain. A dimensionally normalized quadrupolar tide reveals separate equilibrium fold and oscillatory thresholds, including coexisting stable and unstable stationary branches. Finite donor synchronization introduces an additional oscillatory stability frontier. The model recovers the classical Roche and gravitational radiation limits, while the calculated orbital period derivatives are consistent with published binary timing measurements within their combined observational and model uncertainties. These results specify the torque amplitude, restoring stiffness, and synchronization rate needed for local stability, providing quantitative targets for stellar tidal calculations and the interpretation of interacting binaries in the millihertz gravitational wave band.

AI.tldr: This paper builds a conservation-based dynamical stability frontier for interacting binary stars that separates stationary mass transfer from restoration of a perturbed contact state, and applies it to conservative white dwarf binaries with direct impact accretion.
AI.motivation: Existing treatments of contact binary stability do not clearly distinguish genuinely stationary mass transfer from the dynamical restoration of a perturbed contact configuration. The authors aim to establish a rigorous dynamical criterion and quantitative targets (torque amplitude, restoring stiffness, synchronization rate) for local stability in interacting binaries.
AI.method: The formalism couples Roche-lobe overflow, stream angular momentum, gravitational radiation, and both stellar spin reservoirs. From the contact equations the required orbital return torque is derived; an exact Jacobian identity gives the restoring gradient and an oscillatory stability boundary. A dimensionally normalized quadrupolar tide is introduced to separate equilibrium fold and oscillatory thresholds, and finite donor synchronization is included as an additional oscillatory frontier.
AI.result: The computed white dwarf domain yields an oscillatory stability boundary, and the normalized tide reveals distinct equilibrium fold and oscillatory thresholds with coexisting stable and unstable stationary branches; finite synchronization adds a further oscillatory frontier. The model recovers the classical Roche and gravitational radiation limits, and calculated orbital period derivatives agree with published binary timing measurements within combined observational and model uncertainties.
AI.conclusion: The results specify the torque amplitude, restoring stiffness, and synchronization rate required for local stability, providing quantitative benchmarks for stellar tidal calculations and for interpreting interacting binaries in the millihertz gravitational wave band.

title: Nearby M&M Binaries Uncovered with the Gaia Multipeak Fraction and Speckle Interferometry
summary: Multipeak fraction is a strong indicator of stellar multiplicity with subarcsecond angular separation in the Gaia DR3 catalog. We select 18 sources with multipeak fraction above 5% among stars possibly in the 20 pc solar neighborhood with as yet unconfirmed binarity. We successfully resolve eleven systems of M-type dwarf components in speckle interferometric observations with a 2.5 m telescope at the Caucasian Mountain Observatory of Sternberg Astronomical Institute, Moscow State University. The tentatively estimated companion masses lie in the 0.09 -- 0.23 $M_\odot$ range. All six sources with a multipeak fraction of 6--8% are unresolved, suggesting an observational bias that affects nearby stars.

AI.tldr: Using the Gaia DR3 multipeak fraction as a multiplicity indicator, the authors resolved 11 of 18 candidate nearby (20 pc) binaries into M-dwarf pairs via speckle interferometry at a 2.5 m telescope; companion masses are ~0.09–0.23 M_sun, and all six sources with a 6–8% multipeak fraction remained unresolved, hinting at an observational bias for nearby stars.
AI.motivation: The multipeak fraction in the Gaia DR3 catalog is a strong indicator of subarcsecond stellar multiplicity, and stars in the 20 pc solar neighborhood with high multipeak fractions but still-unconfirmed binarity present an opportunity to test this indicator and to discover new close companions.
AI.method: Selection of 18 sources with multipeak fraction >5% among possible 20 pc neighborhood stars lacking confirmed binarity, followed by speckle interferometric observations with a 2.5 m telescope at the Caucasian Mountain Observatory (Sternberg Astronomical Institute, MSU).
AI.result: Eleven systems were resolved, all with M-type dwarf components; tentatively estimated companion masses fall in the 0.09–0.23 M_sun range. All six sources with a multipeak fraction of 6–8% were unresolved.
AI.conclusion: The Gaia DR3 multipeak fraction successfully predicts subarcsecond multiplicity, but the failure to resolve any of the 6–8% multipeak-fraction sources points to an observational bias affecting nearby stars, implying that the indicator's predictive power is mass/separation- and distance-dependent and requires interferometric follow-up to calibrate.

title: ASASSN-15af: An Eclipsing Cataclysmic Variable above the Period Gap Showing Both Positive and Negative Superhump-like Signals
comment: Accepted for publication in the Astronomical Journal. 16 pages, 9 figures, and 4 tables
summary: We present a photometric study of ASASSN-15af (TIC~231050794), combining TESS full-frame-image photometry from the TEQUILA project with 2-minute SPOC light curves and archival ASAS-SN and ATLAS monitoring over 4400~d. The long-term light curve shows recurrent dwarf-nova outbursts, establishing ASASSN-15af as a high-inclination eclipsing dwarf nova above the canonical period gap. From 391 quiescent eclipses, we derive the working ephemeris $T(E)=2139.76108(3)+0.14982063(2)\,E$ (BTJD), corresponding to $P_{\rm orb}=3.596$~hr. A quadratic fit is formally better, but the timings sample only three widely separated epochs, so we regard the apparent O--C curvature as tentative. In quiescence, the out-of-eclipse waveform is dominated by a stable $2f_{\rm orb}$ component, consistent with a substantial ellipsoidal contribution from the donor; during the Sector~96 outburst, its fractional amplitude decreases by $\simeq66\%$, consistent with dilution by the brightened disk. The outburst-only signals occur at periods $\sim1.6\%$ shorter than $P_{\rm orb}$ in Sector~2 and $\sim3.1\%$ longer in Sector~96, consistent with negative- and positive-superhump-like modulations, respectively. Because each is detected in only one outburst, their recurrence remains to be established. Their period-offset ratio, $φ\simeq0.51$, is consistent with empirical trends among systems showing both modes, while the inferred superhump-based mass ratios span $q\simeq0.06$--$0.24$. During the Sector~96 outburst, the eclipse deepens by $ΔD=0.196\pm0.028$ and its centroid shifts earlier by $Δt_{\rm c}=-66.6\pm7.3$~s, indicating a redistribution of accretion-powered light. These results identify ASASSN-15af as an above-gap eclipsing dwarf nova with a dynamically variable accretion disk; spectroscopy is needed to constrain the mass ratio.

AI.tldr: ASASSN-15af is confirmed as a high-inclination eclipsing dwarf nova above the period gap (P_orb = 3.596 hr) with a dynamically variable accretion disk.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to characterize ASASSN-15af (TIC 231050794) photometrically, establishing its nature as an eclipsing dwarf nova, measuring its orbital period, and probing disk variability across outburst and quiescence.
AI.method: Combined TESS full-frame-image photometry (TEQUILA), 2-minute SPOC light curves, and archival ASAS-SN/ATLAS data over ~4400 d. Derived an ephemeris from 391 quiescent eclipses, analyzed out-of-eclipse waveforms, searched for superhump-like signals, and measured eclipse depth and centroid shifts.
AI.result: Ephemeris T(E)=2139.76108(3)+0.14982063(2)E gives P_orb = 3.596 hr. A tentative O–C curvature (quadratic favored, but only three epochs). Stable 2f_orb modulation in quiescence (ellipsoidal), whose fractional amplitude drops ~66% during the Sector 96 outburst. Outburst-only signals at ~1.6% shorter (Sector 2, negative superhump) and ~3.1% longer (Sector 96, positive superhump) than P_orb, with offset ratio φ≈0.51 and inferred q≈0.06–0.24. Eclipse deepens by ΔD=0.196±0.028 and centroid shifts earlier by Δt_c=−66.6±7.3 s during outburst.
AI.conclusion: ASASSN-15af is an above-gap eclipsing dwarf nova with a dynamically variable accretion disk; spectroscopy is required to constrain the mass ratio.

title: Radial Evolution of a Corotating Interaction Region from a High-Resolution MHD Simulation
summary: Corotating interaction regions (CIRs) are large-scale structures formed by fast--slow solar wind interaction, playing a crucial role in heliospheric dynamics and space weather. However, the evolution of individual CIRs and their full three-dimensional morphology remain poorly understood. We investigate the radial evolution of a single CIR using a high-resolution simulation combined with a backmapping method. The simulation reproduces the major plasma and magnetic signatures observed by Wind at 1~AU and by MAVEN and Tianwen-1 at $\sim$1.6~AU. The CIR exhibits a warped, shell-like spiral structure tilted relative to the heliospheric current sheet, consistent with theoretical predictions. During its developing stage, geometric changes are modest, and the radial scalings of velocity ($V_r \propto r^{0.02}$), density ($N \propto r^{-2.00}$), magnetic field ($B_{\rm total} \propto r^{-1.74}$), and temperature ($T \propto r^{-0.97}$) are comparable to those of the background solar wind. In the mature stage, the CIR drifts in longitude and expands toward high latitudes, while its longitudinal and latitudinal widths decrease with distance. The full-domain scalings change markedly to $V_r \propto r^{0.13}$, $N \propto r^{-1.91}$, $B_{\rm total} \propto r^{0.35}$, and $T \propto r^{-0.52}$, differing from both the background wind and the ecliptic-plane CIR. This study quantifies the radial evolution of a CIR from formation to maturity and highlights the importance of its three-dimensional structure in characterizing its morphology and dynamics.

AI.tldr: Using a high-resolution simulation with a backmapping method, the radial evolution of a single corotating interaction region (CIR) is traced from formation to maturity, revealing a warped shell-like spiral morphology and stage-dependent radial scalings distinct from the background solar wind.
AI.motivation: CIRs, formed by fast–slow solar wind interaction, are key to heliospheric dynamics and space weather, yet the evolution of individual CIRs and their full three-dimensional morphology remain poorly understood.
AI.method: A high-resolution simulation combined with a backmapping method is used to investigate the radial evolution of a single CIR, validated against in situ observations from Wind at 1 AU and MAVEN and Tianwen-1 at ~1.6 AU.
AI.result: The simulation reproduces the major plasma and magnetic signatures observed. The CIR shows a warped, shell-like spiral structure tilted relative to the heliospheric current sheet, consistent with theory. In the developing stage, scalings (V_r ∝ r^0.02, N ∝ r^-2.00, B_total ∝ r^-1.74, T ∝ r^-0.97) are comparable to the background wind; in the mature stage, the CIR drifts in longitude, expands to high latitudes with shrinking longitudinal/latitudinal widths, and full-domain scalings shift markedly (V_r ∝ r^0.13, N ∝ r^-1.91, B_total ∝ r^0.35, T ∝ r^-0.52).
AI.conclusion: The study quantifies the radial evolution of a CIR from formation to maturity and underscores the importance of its three-dimensional structure in characterizing CIR morphology and dynamics.

title: Disentangling Magnetospheric and Colliding-Wind X-ray and Radio Emission in the Post-Mass-Transfer Magnetic Massive Binary Plaskett's Star
comment: 24 pages, 17 figures, 5 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Plaskett's star is an O+O binary system harboring a kG-order magnetic field associated with the broad-lined secondary. It is the only O-type star believed to host a centrifugally supported magnetosphere. We present orbital- and rotational-phase resolved X-ray and low-frequency radio observations of Plaskett's star. X-ray observations were taken with Chandra using the High Energy Transmission Grating Spectrometer (HETGS), while the radio observations come from uGMRT and VLA. The X-ray light curve shows rotational modulation according to the magnetic component's rotation period, with maximum flux near magnetic minima. We confirm the decline in flux near orbital phase 0.5 where the slow rotator primary is in front of its magnetic companion. We used the $f/i$ ratios of Si XIII and Mg XI from high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy to infer the location of the plasma emitting X-rays. We find no statistically significant variation in line widths or centroid shifts with either orbital or rotational phase; however, given instrumental limitations, this non-detection may partly reflect observational constraints, while still suggesting a complex and extended X-ray emitting plasma distribution. We could not detect the star in the low-frequency radio bands (0.6--1.5 GHz). Re-analysis of existing Very Large Array data reveals an additional detection at 3 GHz, consistent with a nonthermal contribution predicted by magnetospheric models, although no direct signature was obtained. At low frequencies, nonthermal emission from the magnetosphere and the colliding-wind region is likely suppressed by free-free absorption in the winds of one or both components.

AI.tldr: Phase-resolved Chandra HETGS X-ray and uGMRT/VLA radio observations of Plaskett's star confirm rotational X-ray modulation, place the hot plasma via line-ratio diagnostics, and find no low-frequency radio detection, consistent with free-free absorption of magnetospheric and wind-collision emission.
AI.motivation: Plaskett's star is the only O-type star thought to host a centrifugally supported magnetosphere, associated with its magnetic broad-lined secondary, yet its high-energy and radio behavior as a function of orbital and rotational phase is poorly constrained. The authors aim to localize the X-ray emitting plasma and test magnetospheric versus colliding-wind emission models.
AI.method: Orbital- and rotational-phase resolved X-ray spectroscopy with Chandra/HETGS, using Si XIII and Mg XI forbidden-to-interstrip (f/i) ratios to locate the plasma and searching for phase-dependent line-width and centroid shifts. Complementary low-frequency radio observations (0.6–1.5 GHz) with uGMRT and VLA, plus re-analysis of archival VLA 3 GHz data.
AI.result: The X-ray light curve shows rotational modulation at the magnetic component's period, peaking near magnetic minima, and confirms a flux decline near orbital phase 0.5 when the slowly rotating primary occults the magnetic companion. No statistically significant phase variation in line widths or centroids is found, though instrumental limits weaken this non-detection; the implied plasma is complex and extended. No low-frequency radio detection was obtained; archival VLA data reveal a 3 GHz detection consistent with a nonthermal magnetospheric contribution, without a direct signature.
AI.conclusion: X-ray emission from Plaskett's star is modulated by the magnetic secondary's rotation and attenuated at superior conjunction, indicating magnetically influenced, spatially extended hot plasma. Low-frequency nonthermal emission from the magnetosphere and colliding-wind region is most likely suppressed by free-free absorption in the stellar winds.

title: Kepler as an accidental heliospheric imager: Thomson-scattered solar-wind structure in four years of background photometry
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures (1 animated; animation included as an ancillary file). Submitted to ApJ. Companion paper on comets in Kepler background photometry
summary: Kepler recorded several thousand dedicated sky-background pixels per detector output every 29.4 min from 2009 May to 2013 May while staring at a fixed 12-degree field at ecliptic latitude +65 degrees. From this archive we isolate a large-scale layer that measures brightness variations relative to an 8-day running median. This layer contains fluctuations of 0.02-0.1 electrons per second per pixel (about 1e-17 of the mean solar surface brightness) that sweep across the field in a day or less. Four lines of evidence show that these are sunlight Thomson-scattered by solar-wind electrons. (1) The sweeps propagate away from the Sun (84 percent within 45 degrees of the anti-solar direction; 25 percent expected by chance), and their direction follows the Sun through each quarter and across all 16 spacecraft rolls. (2) The field brightness correlates with the near-Earth (OMNI) proton density within a day of zero lag (r = 0.19, p < 1/150), but not with the energetic-proton flux. (3) Time-elongation maps show fronts moving outward at a median 15 degrees per day, as forward models of radially moving density structures predict. (4) The amplitude is about one third of a parameter-free Thomson-scattering prediction and varies by a factor of about 3 over the year, as predicted. Half of the scattered light comes from within 0.4-0.7 AU of the spacecraft. Fronts are strongest in slow wind. Kepler's background pixels thus provide a four-year, high-cadence, out-of-ecliptic record of solar-wind structure near 1 AU. Standard Kepler processing removes these signals, changing stellar light curves by less than about 1 ppm.

title: Multi-year forecasting of F10.7 and F30 solar radio flux using an adaptive Kalman filter and hemispheric solar activity
summary: The F10.7 and F30 radio flux indices drive thermospheric and radiation-environment models, and long-term predictions are needed for satellite mission planning, orbital-lifetime estimates, and re-entry assessments. We develop multi-year predictions of both indices for lead times of 1 to 84 months using three complementary contributions. First, we apply the McNish-Lincoln (M&L) method and demonstrate its predictive skill over multi-year horizons, with RMSE of 11-22 sfu for F10.7 and 7-14 sfu for F30. RMSE largely stabilizes after roughly 36 months, indicating near-constant forecast skill over the seven-year horizon. Accuracy also depends strongly on the solar-cycle phase at which the forecast is issued, with the most favorable starting intervals occurring progressively earlier in the cycle for longer lead times. Second, we update the initial predictions using an adaptive Kalman filter with noise statistics identification, which assimilates the latest monthly observations to reconstruct the current smoothed flux, remove the delay introduced by centered smoothing, and improve solar-cycle state estimation, reducing forecast errors by up to 70%. Third, we introduce synthetic hemispheric components of solar radio flux to account for the separate evolution of the northern and southern hemispheres, and incorporate them into a hemispheric M&L formulation. Compared with the initial M&L predictions, it reduces RMSE by up to 55% for F10.7 and 58% for F30, showing that hemispheric asymmetry contains predictive information lost in the full-disk index. These results extend solar-cycle forecasting to multi-year timescales relevant for long-term space-weather applications and operational planning.

AI.tldr: Multi-year (1–84 month) forecasts of the F10.7 and F30 solar radio flux indices are developed using the McNish-Lincoln method, an adaptive Kalman filter, and synthetic hemispheric components, achieving RMSE of 11–22 sfu (F10.7) and 7–14 sfu (F30).
AI.motivation: F10.7 and F30 flux indices drive thermospheric and radiation-environment models, so long-term predictions are needed for satellite mission planning, orbital-lifetime estimation, and re-entry assessment.
AI.method: Three complementary contributions: (1) McNish-Lincoln (M&L) method applied over multi-year horizons; (2) an adaptive Kalman filter with noise-statistics identification that assimilates monthly observations to reconstruct the smoothed flux, remove centered-smoothing delay, and improve solar-cycle state estimation; (3) synthetic hemispheric components of solar radio flux incorporated into a hemispheric M&L formulation to capture north-south asymmetry.
AI.result: M&L yields RMSE of 11–22 sfu for F10.7 and 7–14 sfu for F30; RMSE stabilizes after ~36 months, indicating near-constant skill over seven years, and accuracy depends strongly on the solar-cycle phase at forecast issuance. The Kalman filter reduces errors by up to 70%. The hemispheric formulation reduces RMSE by up to 55% (F10.7) and 58% (F30).
AI.conclusion: Hemispheric asymmetry carries predictive information lost in the full-disk index, and the combined approach extends solar-cycle forecasting to multi-year timescales relevant for long-term space-weather applications and operational planning.

title: Distinguishing between flaring and non-flaring solar active regions with height-dependent polarity inversion line lengths
summary: Polarity Inversion Lines (PILs) are regions on the Sun's surface across which the vertical magnetic field changes polarity. This study examines whether the total length of PILs within a height range of 0-3.24 Mm above the photosphere can distinguish between strongly flaring active regions, with at least one flare of GOES (Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite) class M1 or higher, and non-flaring active regions, where the strongest flare remains weaker than GOES class C1. Using magnetic field extrapolations on a dataset of 40 active regions, the study compares the 48-hr evolution of the total PIL length prior to the first major flare in strongly flaring regions with identical time intervals in non-flaring regions. It is seen that the 48-hr maximum of the total PIL length differs clearly between the two groups. This distinction becomes stronger at heights about 1-2 Mm above the photosphere. It is further seen that at about 1.8 Mm, the maximum value of the total PIL length, for around (i) 78 percent of weakly flaring regions (where the strongest flare is a C-class flare) and (ii) 96 percent of non-flaring active regions, is less than the minimum value of the total PIL length of their strongly flaring counterparts. These results suggest that strongly flaring active regions may be distinguishable from non-flaring or weakly flaring ones using thresholds on PIL lengths in the lower solar atmosphere. Further, this study highlights the importance of studying chromospheric magnetic fields in flare precursor investigations.

AI.tldr: The 48-hour maximum of total Polarity Inversion Line (PIL) length in the 0–3.24 Mm height range distinguishes strongly flaring active regions from non-flaring ones, with the strongest separation occurring ~1–2 Mm above the photosphere.
AI.motivation: To test whether the total length of PILs in the lower solar atmosphere (0–3.24 Mm) can serve as a discriminator between strongly flaring active regions (≥M1) and non-flaring ones (<C1), thereby advancing flare-precursor diagnostics based on chromospheric magnetic fields.
AI.method: Magnetic field extrapolations over 40 active regions; comparison of the 48-hr evolution of total PIL length prior to the first major flare in strongly flaring regions versus matched time intervals in non-flaring regions, analyzed as a function of height.
AI.result: The 48-hr maximum total PIL length clearly differs between groups, with the distinction peaking ~1–2 Mm above the photosphere. At ~1.8 Mm, this maximum lies below the minimum value of strongly flaring counterparts for ~78% of weakly flaring (C-class) regions and ~96% of non-flaring regions.
AI.conclusion: Thresholds on PIL length in the lower solar atmosphere may allow strongly flaring active regions to be distinguished from non-flaring or weakly flaring ones, underscoring the importance of chromospheric magnetic fields in flare-precursor studies.

title: Inferring accretion bursts in intermediate-mass protostars from asteroseismic imprints
summary: During star formation, objects may gain the majority of their final mass through regular and intense bursts of mass accretion. For bursts of the FU Orionis-type (FUor), accretion rates can climb to $10^{-3} \ \text{M}_\odot \text{yr}^{-1}$ during short windows of time, amounting to just a few percent of the main accretion phase. To study the occurrence of such events observationally, signatures of the current accretion bursts and tracers of recent bursts are crucial. We investigate the potential to identify accretion bursts in protostars and pre-main sequence stars of intermediate mass using asteroseismology. We use the stellar structure and evolution code MESA to evolve stellar models from the protostellar seed phase of $0.01 \ \text{M}_\odot$ and $1.5 \ \text{R}_\odot$ up to $4.0 \ \text{M}_\odot$ with a constant accretion rate of $10^{-6} \ \text{M}_\odot \text{yr}^{-1}$. A single accretion burst is initialized during the accretion phase. The stellar oscillation code GYRE is employed to compute the resulting asteroseismic properties of the models. Accretion bursts of up to $10^{-3} \ \text{M}_\odot \text{yr}^{-1}$ are sufficient to cause the convective cores of the models to recede, leaving behind a chemical trace which manifests itself in the form of quasi-periodic dips in the g-mode period spacing. This effect is strongest during the outburst, but also lingers for up to 475 years before the convective core is re-established and the dips are gone. Our experiment shows that a single accretion burst leaves an imprint in the deep interiors of protostars and pre-MS stars of intermediate mass, and that this imprint can be captured with asteroseismology. Our results are most conclusive for burst magnitudes greater than $1\times10^{-4} \ \text{M}_\odot \text{yr}^{-1}$, corresponding to FUor-type bursts.

AI.tldr: Using MESA and GYRE, the authors show that a single FUor-type accretion burst recedes the convective core of intermediate-mass protostars/pre-main-sequence stars, leaving a quasi-periodic dip signature in g-mode period spacings that persists up to 475 years and is asteroseismically detectable.
AI.motivation: Objects may acquire most of their final mass via regular, intense accretion bursts (FUor-type, up to 1e-3 Msun/yr), but observational signatures of current and recent bursts are needed to assess how common such events are; the authors test whether asteroseismology can identify them in intermediate-mass protostars and pre-MS stars.
AI.method: Stellar structure/evolution models computed with MESA, evolved from a 0.01 Msun, 1.5 Rsun protostellar seed up to 4.0 Msun at a constant 1e-6 Msun/yr accretion rate, with a single accretion burst initialized during the accretion phase; oscillation properties derived with the GYRE code to obtain asteroseismic diagnostics.
AI.result: Bursts up to 1e-3 Msun/yr cause the convective cores to recede, leaving a chemical trace manifested as quasi-periodic dips in the g-mode period spacing. The effect is strongest during the outburst and lingers for up to 475 years until the convective core is re-established and the dips vanish; results are most conclusive for burst magnitudes above 1e-4 Msun/yr, i.e., FUor-type bursts.
AI.conclusion: A single accretion burst leaves a detectable imprint in the deep interiors of intermediate-mass protostars and pre-MS stars that can be captured with asteroseismology, providing a potential probe of FUor-type burst events.

title: Zeeman-Doppler imaging of active young Suns. New surface magnetic field maps for BE Cet, HN Peg, and kappa1 Cet
summary: Studying the magnetic activity of young solar analogues is important for understanding the dynamo mechanisms of the Sun and other late-type stars. We aimed to determine the surface magnetic field topology of four stars, analogues to the young Sun. This will contribute to long-term studies of the evolution of magnetic activity on different timescales of these targets. We obtained high resolution spectropolarimetric measurements with the HARPSpol instrument mounted at the ESO 3.6m telescope in the epoch 2021.6, and the SOFIN instrument, mounted on the 2.56m NOT telescope in epochs 2017.4 and 2021.5. The signal-to-noise ratio of the observations was boosted with least squares deconvolution. The surface magnetic field maps were calculated with the Zeeman-Doppler imaging technique. The magnetic field is decomposed into spherical harmonic expansions, allowing us to quantify the contributions from the axisymmetric and non-axisymmetric components, as well as the poloidal and toroidal fields. Out of the four stars observed (BE Cet, HN Peg, kappa1 Cet, V1358 Ori), three (BE Cet, HN Peg, kappa1 Cet) show clear signs of magnetic fields. Only one star, BE Cet shows clear evidence for the dominance of non-axisymmetric modes and the poloidal field being more dominant than the toroidal. HN Peg also shows signs of a stronger poloidal than a toroidal field, indicating an α^2 dynamo, where the convective turbulence effects dominate over the differential rotation. The magnetic field of V1358 Ori could not be reliably reconstructed.

AI.tldr: High-resolution spectropolarimetry and Zeeman-Doppler imaging reveal magnetic field topologies of four young solar analogue stars; three show detectable fields, with BE Cet and HN Peg exhibiting poloidal-dominated fields consistent with an α² dynamo.
AI.motivation: Understanding the dynamo mechanisms of the Sun and other late-type stars requires studying magnetic activity in young solar analogues, and long-term monitoring of such targets is needed to trace the evolution of magnetic activity across different timescales.
AI.method: High-resolution spectropolarimetric observations were obtained with HARPSpol (ESO 3.6m) at epoch 2021.6 and SOFIN (NOT 2.56m) at epochs 2017.4 and 2021.5. Signal-to-noise was enhanced via least squares deconvolution, and surface magnetic field maps were reconstructed using Zeeman-Doppler imaging. The field was decomposed into spherical harmonic expansions to quantify axisymmetric/non-axisymmetric and poloidal/toroidal contributions.
AI.result: Of the four targets (BE Cet, HN Peg, kappa1 Cet, V1358 Ori), three (BE Cet, HN Peg, kappa1 Cet) show clear magnetic field signatures. BE Cet uniquely shows dominant non-axisymmetric modes with a poloidal field stronger than the toroidal. HN Peg also shows a stronger poloidal than toroidal field, indicating an α² dynamo where convective turbulence effects dominate over differential rotation. The field of V1358 Ori could not be reliably reconstructed.
AI.conclusion: The results provide surface magnetic field topologies for young solar analogues, supporting an α² dynamo interpretation for at least BE Cet and HN Peg, and contribute to long-term studies of magnetic activity evolution. One target (V1358 Ori) remains unresolved, likely requiring further observations.

title: Geometric tracking of a halo CME using full-circle wide-field views from PUNCH
summary: We tracked the large, geoeffective halo coronal mass ejection (CME) of 2025-May-31 across the very wide field of view of the Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere (PUNCH) mission, as a proof of concept for data-informed forecasting of CME arrival times at Earth. using simple point-and-click measurement of the front location as far as 47 degrees away from the Sun itself, we constrained an analytic "ludicrous ice-cream cone" geometric model with just three parameters: position angle, off-Earth-Sun angle, and propagation speed. We show that the model is sufficient to capture the bulk envelope of the CME, and also insufficient to capture the complexity of the CME's evolution. We generated simulated arrival-time forecasts for the CME by extrapolating the constant-velocity propagation to determine the time of impact with Earth. These "retro-forecasts" converged to within 30 +/- 15 minutes of the actual arrival time, 8 hours prior to arrival. The convergence was marked by a clear inflection point in the curve of predicted-arrival-time vs time-of-forecast. We conclude that continuous wide-field tracking is sufficiently powerful to enable even crude models to substantially improve arrival-time forecasting precision, and discuss future work required both to validate this single-event result and to extend it to more sophisticated analyses.

AI.tldr: Using PUNCH's wide field of view, the authors track the 2025-May-31 halo CME out to 47 degrees from the Sun and constrain a three-parameter "ludicrous ice-cream cone" model to produce retro-forecasts that converged to within 30 +/- 15 minutes of the actual Earth arrival time, 8 hours before impact.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate a proof of concept that data-informed forecasting of CME arrival times at Earth can be improved by continuous wide-field tracking, leveraging the extended view of the PUNCH mission.
AI.method: Point-and-click measurement of the CME front location out to 47 degrees from the Sun constrained an analytic "ludicrous ice-cream cone" geometric model with three parameters (position angle, off-Earth-Sun angle, propagation speed); constant-velocity propagation was extrapolated to generate simulated arrival-time forecasts ("retro-forecasts").
AI.result: The model captured the bulk envelope of the CME but not its full evolutionary complexity. Retro-forecasts converged to within 30 +/- 15 minutes of the actual arrival time 8 hours prior to arrival, with convergence marked by a clear inflection point in predicted-arrival-time versus time-of-forecast.
AI.conclusion: Continuous wide-field tracking is sufficiently powerful to enable even crude geometric models to substantially improve CME arrival-time forecasting precision; future work is needed to validate this single-event result and extend it to more sophisticated analyses.

title: Ca II IRT activity indices from $Gaia$ spectroscopy: a baseline method for photospheric contribution estimates
comment: 14 pages, 12 figures, 4 tables. Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: The $Gaia$ high-resolution spectroscopic observations using Radial Velocity Spectrometer offers a unique opportunity to study stellar Ca II infrared triplet (IRT) activity. A key step in estimating activity indices is subtracting the photospheric contribution. The canonical template-based method often fails because, for many stars, the observed line cores are deeper than the model predictions, which prevents valid activity measurements. In this work, we explore an alternative approach that constructs a baseline from less active stars as a function of effective temperature (and metallicity) to represent the photospheric contribution. Our results show that, for dwarf stars, compared with the canonical method, the baseline method not only yields far more objects with valid activity measurements, but also avoids many extremely low and unreliable values (e.g., log$R'_{\rm IRT} \lesssim -6$). The Ca II IRT activity indices derived from the baseline method correlate well with other activity proxies, confirming their reliability as activity indicators. Furthermore, they show a relation with stellar rotation, not only recovering the typical rotation--activity relation, but also revealing fine structures that may be associated with different regimes in gyrochronology. Our findings suggest that the baseline method can serve as a robust alternative for deriving accurate activity estimates, and will be particularly useful for obtaining activity indices for tens of millions of stars with the upcoming $Gaia$ Data Release 4.

AI.tldr: A baseline (empirical photospheric) method, built from less active stars as a function of Teff and metallicity, replaces the failing canonical template-subtraction for Ca II IRT activity indices, yielding more reliable, rotation-correlated activity measures for dwarf stars and scaling to Gaia DR4.
AI.motivation: Gaia's Radial Velocity Spectrometer enables large-scale study of stellar Ca II infrared triplet (IRT) activity, but estimating activity indices requires removing the photospheric contribution. The canonical template-based subtraction often fails because observed line cores are deeper than model predictions for many stars, preventing valid activity measurements.
AI.method: The authors construct a baseline from less active stars as a function of effective temperature (and metallicity) to represent the photospheric contribution, as an alternative to canonical template subtraction, and compare the two on dwarf stars while validating against other activity proxies and stellar rotation.
AI.result: For dwarf stars, the baseline method yields far more objects with valid activity measurements than the canonical method and avoids many extremely low, unreliable values (e.g., logR'_IRT ≲ -6). Derived Ca II IRT indices correlate well with other activity proxies, confirming reliability, and show a rotation relation that recovers the typical rotation–activity relation while revealing fine structures potentially tied to different gyrochronology regimes.
AI.conclusion: The baseline method is a robust alternative for deriving accurate Ca II IRT activity estimates, offering broader valid coverage and avoiding spurious low values. It will be particularly useful for obtaining activity indices for tens of millions of stars in the upcoming Gaia Data Release 4.

title: XRISM/Xtend detection of solar wind charge exchange induced by multiple coronal mass ejections in 2024 August
comment: 11 pages, 12 figures, 2 tables; published online in PASJ; scheduled for publication in Vol. 78, Issue 6
summary: Solar wind charge exchange (SWCX) emission is often a major component of the soft X-ray background, but it also provides a remote diagnostic of the composition and ionization state of solar wind plasma. We present an analysis of a SWCX event observed with XRISM/Xtend during 2024 August 9-13. The event occurred during intense solar activity with multiple flares, including an X1.3-class solar flare, and associated coronal mass ejections (CMEs). We found a clear enhancement in the 0.3-3.0 keV count rate that occurred nearly simultaneously with an increase in the solar wind proton flux measured by ACE. We fitted the spectrum during the enhancement period with a set of Gaussian emission lines. In addition to the commonly detected C, N, and O lines, we detected Ne, Mg, Si, and Fe lines at $>15σ$ significance. We extracted two characteristic periods within the enhanced interval based on the CME arrival timeline. The O$_{\rm VIII}$/Si$_{\rm XIII}$ line ratio changed significantly between the two periods, suggesting contributions from multiple CME components. We then applied the AtomDB charge exchange model with a multi-temperature setup. The estimated ionization temperatures for Ne, Mg, Si, and Fe increased with the peak soft X-ray flux of the associated solar flares. This trend suggests that coronal heating becomes more efficient for more intense flares. Meanwhile, the ionization temperatures were lower than typical flare electron temperatures, implying that CME plasma may have been released into interplanetary space under non-equilibrium ionization conditions. We also found an indication of an inverse-FIP pattern, with reduced relative abundances of Si and S. These results demonstrate that XRISM/Xtend can diagnose the coronal plasma through SWCX emission, including heavy ions such as Ne, Mg, and Si, which are difficult to measure with current in-situ instruments (e.g., ACE satellite).

AI.tldr: Using XRISM/Xtend, the authors analyzed a solar wind charge exchange (SWCX) event from 2024 August 9–13, detecting C, N, O, Ne, Mg, Si, and Fe lines (>15σ) and inferring ionization temperatures and abundances of CME-related plasma.
AI.motivation: SWCX emission dominates the soft X-ray background but can be used as a remote probe of solar wind composition and ionization state. Heavy ions such as Ne, Mg, and Si are hard to measure with in-situ instruments like ACE, so a high-resolution X-ray observatory can fill this gap.
AI.method: Spectral analysis of the 0.3–3.0 keV enhancement with XRISM/Xtend during a period of intense solar activity (including an X1.3 flare and CMEs). The enhancement spectrum was fitted with Gaussian emission lines; two characteristic periods were defined from the CME arrival timeline; the AtomDB charge exchange model with a multi-temperature setup was applied to derive ionization temperatures and relative abundances.
AI.result: A clear count-rate enhancement coincided with an increase in ACE proton flux. Beyond C, N, O lines, Ne, Mg, Si, and Fe lines were detected at >15σ. The O VIII/Si XIII ratio changed significantly between the two periods, implying contributions from multiple CME components. Ionization temperatures of Ne, Mg, Si, and Fe increased with the peak soft X-ray flux of the associated flares, but remained below typical flare electron temperatures. An indication of an inverse-FIP pattern (reduced Si and S abundances) was found.
AI.conclusion: Coronal heating appears more efficient for more intense flares; CME plasma may be released into interplanetary space under non-equilibrium ionization conditions. XRISM/Xtend can diagnose coronal plasma via SWCX emission, including heavy ions inaccessible to current in-situ instruments.

title: Simulating high-speed solar wind streams from coronal holes using an L5-L1 configuration of Lagrangian points
summary: Coronal holes (CHs) are known to be sources of high-speed solar wind streams (HSSs), yet the physical mechanisms linking CH position and characteristics to solar wind (SW) behaviour remain unclear. Our results reveal that the latitude of CHs, especially smaller ones, combined with the heliographic latitude of the solar disk's central point (B0 angle), plays a critical role in driving discrepancies in SW velocity across the heliosphere. To investigate this, we use archival data from STEREO-B, STEREO-A, and Earth to simulate an L5-L1 configuration, where L5 is a vantage point approximately behind Earth in its orbit (as proposed for the Vigil mission), and L1 is between Earth and the Sun where SW measurements are typically taken. We use these insights to develop a predictive algorithm for HSSs, beginning with an analysis of the separation angle and distances between L5 and L1. We then introduce a predictive indicator and empirical criteria based on CH properties and the B0 angle to adjust for changes in SW velocity at L1. Our results show that the L5 viewpoint demonstrates the capability to significantly improve the accuracy and lead times of HSS predictions, enhancing our understanding of the CH-HSS relationship and potentially improving space weather forecasting.

AI.tldr: Coronal hole (CH) latitude and the solar B0 angle explain discrepancies in solar wind velocity across the heliosphere; an L5 vantage point (simulated with STEREO data) enables improved high-speed stream (HSS) prediction accuracy and lead time.
AI.motivation: Although CHs are known sources of high-speed solar wind streams, the physical link between CH position/characteristics and solar wind behaviour remains unclear, and current L1-based HSS forecasting lacks sufficient accuracy and lead time.
AI.method: Archival data from STEREO-B, STEREO-A and Earth are used to emulate an L5–L1 configuration (L5 as an Earth-trailing vantage, as proposed for Vigil; L1 as the near-Earth measurement point). The study analyzes the separation angle and distances between L5 and L1, then develops a predictive algorithm with a predictive indicator and empirical criteria based on CH properties plus the B0 angle to correct for solar wind velocity changes at L1.
AI.result: CH latitude—particularly for smaller CHs—together with the B0 angle critically drives heliospheric SW velocity discrepancies; the L5 viewpoint substantially improves the accuracy and lead times of HSS predictions.
AI.conclusion: L5 observations enhance understanding of the CH–HSS relationship and offer a promising route to improved space weather forecasting.

title: Rotating Polytropic Twins and the Fragmentation Problem
summary: Polytropic n=1 stellar configurations with strong differential rotation have been considered. The so-called twin configurations: stars having almost identical integral characteristics, but clearly structurally different have been found. Hydrodynamic 3D modeling has been performed for two such structures and has shown that these configurations also differ in the dynamic aspect: one of them remains practically stationary, while the other turns out to be unstable with respect to the development of the bar mode and fragmentation. The gravitational wave signal accompanying the fragmentation process has been calculated.

AI.tldr: Twin n=1 polytropic stellar configurations with strong differential rotation—nearly identical global quantities but structurally distinct—were found, and 3D hydrodynamic modeling shows they differ dynamically: one stays quasi-stationary whereas the other is bar-mode unstable and fragments, producing a calculable gravitational-wave signal.
AI.motivation: Differential rotation in polytropic stars may permit non-unique equilibrium solutions (twins) that share almost identical integral characteristics but differ in internal structure; whether such twins are also dynamically distinct, and what observable signatures (e.g., gravitational waves) separate them, is unclear.
AI.method: Construction of n=1 polytropic equilibrium configurations with strong differential rotation, identification of twin pairs, and 3D hydrodynamic simulations of two such structures to assess stability, including analysis of the bar-mode instability, fragmentation, and the associated gravitational-wave emission.
AI.result: The two twin configurations, though nearly identical in integral properties, behave qualitatively differently in dynamics: one remains essentially stationary, while the other is unstable to the bar mode and undergoes fragmentation; the gravitational-wave signal generated during fragmentation was computed.
AI.conclusion: Twin configurations are not only structurally but also dynamically distinguishable, so integral (global) parameters alone cannot determine a star's fate; the dynamical instability and its gravitational-wave signature offer a potential discriminator between otherwise near-degenerate configurations.

title: Mapping the obscured Galactic disk: ERIS J-band low-resolution spectroscopy of 27 Classical Cepheids
comment: Paper accepted for publication in the section "5. Galactic structure, stellar clusters and populations" of Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Classical Cepheids (CCs) are standard candles and key tracers of young stellar populations. However, their use in the most obscured regions is hampered by the high interstellar extinction at optical wavelengths. Near-infrared spectroscopy offers major advantages by greatly reducing absorption corrections and enabling access to regions of the Milky Way that are still poorly sampled. In this work, we determine the atmospheric parameters and abundances of Fe, Mg and Si for a sample of 27 CCs based on observations with ERIS@VLT in J-band low-resolution mode ($R \sim 4000$). Combining PySME with 1D MARCS atmosphere models and non local thermal equilibrium grids, we simultaneous optimise the atmospheric parameters through spectral fitting. This method is validated with a direct comparison with high-resolution optical investigations and re-analysis of archive optical spectra for the targets in common. The results show good consistency in both metallicity and chemical abundances. We obtain mean abundance ratios of $\mathrm{\langle[Mg/Fe]\rangle=0.01\pm0.12~dex}$ and $\mathrm{\langle[Si/Fe]\rangle=0.10\pm0.09~dex}$, in agreement with reference samples. Moreover, we provide for the first time the Mg and Si abundances of 12 CCs. Finally, we have found distinct kinematic properties for two of the most distant Galactic CCs, located at Galactocentric distances of $\mathrm{\approx 28-29~kpc}$ and with extreme values of vertical height, $\mathrm{\approx +4.8~kpc}$ and $\mathrm{\approx -5.3~kpc}$; more data are required to constrain their nature. Our results confirm that J-band spectroscopy at low-resolution can be used as a good diagnostic for the chemical investigation in highly obscured Galactic regions, otherwise inaccessible at optical wavelengths.

AI.tldr: J-band low-resolution (R~4000) ERIS@VLT spectroscopy is used to derive atmospheric parameters and Fe, Mg, Si abundances for 27 classical Cepheids, validated against high-resolution optical data, enabling chemical studies in highly obscured Galactic regions.
AI.motivation: Classical Cepheids are standard candles and tracers of young stellar populations, but optical studies are severely hampered by high interstellar extinction in obscured regions. Near-infrared spectroscopy minimizes absorption corrections and opens poorly sampled Milky Way regions.
AI.method: 27 CCs observed with ERIS@VLT in J-band low-resolution mode (R~4000). Atmospheric parameters and Fe, Mg, Si abundances derived by simultaneously fitting spectra with PySME, 1D MARCS models, and NLTE grids. Method validated via direct comparison with high-resolution optical studies and re-analysis of archival optical spectra for common targets.
AI.result: Good consistency in metallicity and abundances versus optical references. Mean ratios ⟨[Mg/Fe]⟩=0.01±0.12 dex and ⟨[Si/Fe]⟩=0.10±0.09 dex, consistent with reference samples. First Mg and Si abundances for 12 CCs. Two distant CCs (~28–29 kpc Galactocentric, vertical heights ~+4.8 and ~-5.3 kpc) show distinct kinematics.
AI.conclusion: Low-resolution J-band spectroscopy is a valid diagnostic for chemical investigations in highly obscured Galactic regions inaccessible at optical wavelengths; more data are needed to constrain the nature of the two extreme distant Cepheids.

title: All-sky spectroscopic survey of bright δ Scuti stars from TESS Projected rotational velocities and pulsation characteristics
summary: Context. The second most numerous class of pulsating stars -- $δ$ Scuti ($δ$ Sct) -- lack a homogeneous, large-scale spectroscopic sample in the Kepler and TESS era, limiting our understanding of how rotation shapes stellar pulsations. Aims. We analyse projected rotational velocities ($v \sin i$) from high-resolution spectroscopy alongside 2-minute TESS photometry to establish empirical links between stellar rotation and pulsation parameters. Methods. Combining observations from three high-resolution échelle spectrographs with two spectral libraries, we assemble an all-sky sample of 262 $δ$ Sct stars ($R = 25\,000$ to $115\,000$). We derive $v \sin i$ via three independent methods and extract pulsation frequencies and amplitudes from TESS light curves. Results. The $v \sin i$ distribution is unimodal, with a mean of $120.3\text{ km s}^{-1}$ and peak probability at $113.8\text{ km s}^{-1}$. Minimum ($ν_{\rm min}$), dominant ($ν_{\rm dom}$), amplitude-weighted ($ν_{\rm AW}$), and power-weighted ($ν_{\rm PW}$) frequencies decrease with $v \sin i / v_{\rm crit}$, whereas maximum frequency ($ν_{\rm max}$) does not. Fast rotators show a narrower range of photometric and pulsation amplitudes than slow rotators, and their lower mean stellar density ($\barρ$) cannot fully explain the frequency decrease. Calibrating Gaia's $v_{\rm broad}$ against our measurements removes its systematic offset, enabling use across larger $δ$ Sct samples. Multi-spectrum comparisons reveal method discrepancies mainly for fast rotators ($v \sin i > 200\text{ km s}^{-1}$) and inter-spectrograph offsets up to $20\text{ km s}^{-1}$. Conclusions. We present the largest homogeneous high-resolution $v \sin i$ sample for bright $δ$ Sct stars in the TESS era, showing that $v \sin i$ measurements in pulsating stars require careful treatment across instruments and velocity regimes.

AI.tldr: The largest homogeneous high-resolution projected rotational velocity ($v\sin i$) sample of 262 $\delta$ Scuti stars is assembled from three échelle spectrographs and two spectral libraries plus 2-minute TESS photometry; the $v\sin i$ distribution peaks at ~114 km/s, and several pulsation frequencies decrease with $v\sin i/v_{\rm crit}$ while $v_{\rm max}$ does not.
AI.motivation: $\delta$ Scuti stars lack a homogeneous, large-scale spectroscopic sample in the Kepler/TESS era, which limits understanding of how rotation shapes stellar pulsations.
AI.method: Combines three high-resolution échelle spectrographs (R = 25,000–115,000) with two spectral libraries to build an all-sky sample of 262 $\delta$ Sct stars. $v\sin i$ is derived via three independent methods and pulsation frequencies/amplitudes are extracted from TESS light curves; Gaia $v_{\rm broad}$ is calibrated against the measurements and multi-spectrum comparisons assess methodological systematics.
AI.result: The $v\sin i$ distribution is unimodal (mean 120.3 km/s, peak probability at 113.8 km/s). Minimum, dominant, amplitude-weighted and power-weighted frequencies decrease with $v\sin i/v_{\rm crit}$, whereas maximum frequency does not. Fast rotators show a narrower amplitude range than slow rotators, and their lower mean density cannot fully explain the frequency decrease. Calibrating Gaia $v_{\rm broad}$ removes its systematic offset. Method discrepancies arise mainly for fast rotators ($v\sin i$ > 200 km/s), with inter-spectrograph offsets up to 20 km/s.
AI.conclusion: The study provides the largest homogeneous high-resolution $v\sin i$ sample of bright $\delta$ Sct stars in the TESS era and demonstrates that $v\sin i$ measurements in pulsating stars require careful treatment across instruments and velocity regimes.

title: Unexpected Plateau: The Constant $ \rm \log ε(Th/Eu)$ Ratio of Actinide-Boost Stars
summary: The astrophysical site of the rapid neutron-capture process ($r$-process) is still one of the major open questions in astronomy. A key mystery is the origin of the peculiar actinide-to-lanthanide ratio found in the so called actinide-boost stars, with $ \rm \log ε(Th/Eu)>-0.35$. Here we present the largest sample of Th measurements in stars formed in an external galaxy, Gaia Sausage Enceladus. From this sample, we present the three most metal-rich actinide-boost stars discovered to date, $\rm -1.6<[Fe/H]<-1.1$. In addition, we measured Th in a comparison sample of Milky Way stars formed in situ, and compiled Th measurements from the literature which do not account for non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) effects. After applying NLTE corrections to the combined sample, a bimodality in the $\rm\logε(Th/Eu)$ ratio is revealed. Unexpectedly, actinide-boost stars lie on a very narrow $(σ=0.02)$ plateau of $\rm \logε(Th/Eu)=-0.2$, clearly separated from actinide-normal stars. Most (if not all) of the actinide-boost stars in our sample originate from outside the Milky Way. Chemical evolution models show that such a plateau can arise, even at [Fe/H] = $-$1, when a single actinide-rich event dominates the r-process content of a small or gas-depleted system. Combined with other evidence, our results suggest that mergers with neutron stars are the most promising astrophysical site for actinide-boost stars.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the largest Th abundance sample in Gaia Sausage Enceladus stars, discovering the three most metal-rich actinide-boost stars and revealing a narrow logε(Th/Eu) plateau that points to neutron-star mergers as the likely r-process site.
AI.motivation: The astrophysical site of the r-process remains unresolved. A key puzzle is the peculiar actinide-to-lanthanide ratio in actinide-boost stars (log ε(Th/Eu) > -0.35), which lacks a clear explanation.
AI.method: Measurements of Th in the largest sample from an external galaxy (Gaia Sausage Enceladus), plus a comparison sample of in-situ Milky Way stars and literature data. NLTE corrections are applied to the combined sample, and chemical evolution models are used to interpret the observed pattern.
AI.result: The three most metal-rich actinide-boost stars known (-1.6 < [Fe/H] < -1.1) are reported. After NLTE corrections, logε(Th/Eu) shows bimodality: actinide-boost stars lie on a very narrow plateau (σ = 0.02) at logε(Th/Eu) = -0.2, clearly separated from actinide-normal stars. Most actinide-boost stars originate outside the Milky Way. Models show such a plateau can arise at [Fe/H] ≈ -1 when a single actinide-rich event dominates the r-process content of a small or gas-depleted system.
AI.conclusion: Combined with other evidence, the results suggest neutron-star mergers are the most promising astrophysical site for actinide-boost stars.

title: Two new Li-rich dwarf stars in M 4: abundance patterns and possible origins
summary: Context. Li-rich stars are rare, and only 16 are known in globular clusters (GCs), spanning evolutionary stages from the main sequence turnoff to the red giant branch. Their origin is still debated, but GCs provide a unique environment to discriminate among proposed mechanisms for Li enrichment. Aims. We aim to characterise two newly discovered Li-rich dwarf stars, 44606 and 58195, in the GC M 4 (NGC 6121) and investigate their origin among the formation channels proposed in the literature. The previously known Li-rich star in the cluster, namely 37934, was re-analyzed for comparison. Methods. We performed a standard abundance analysis based on 1D model atmospheres in local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) on high-resolution Ultraviolet and Visual Echelle Spectrograph (UVES). We measured the projected rotational velocity and searched for chromospheric activity. Results. We derive A(Li)= 2.58, 2.51 dex for stars 44606 and 58195, respectively, significantly different from the A(Li) distribution of normal dwarfs in M 4. For the known Li-rich star 37934, we obtain A(Li)= 3.01 dex, consistent with previous work. We estimate detailed abundances of 24 species (Li, C, N, O, Na, Mg, Al, Si, S, K, Ca, Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Sr, Y, Zr, Ba, and Nd) in the three stars. None of our targets show detectable rotational broadening or chromospheric activity. Conclusions. The Li-rich stars analysed here are unevolved, ruling out in-situ Li production. Planet engulfment is very unlikely in GCs, and we detect no present-day rotation or activity. By exclusion, the most plausible remaining scenarios involve different types of interaction with a companion, including dynamical interactions, mass transfer, and mergers. Currently, we have not detected a companion.

AI.tldr: Abundance analysis of two newly discovered Li-rich dwarf stars (44606, 58195) in globular cluster M4, plus re-analysis of known Li-rich star 37934, finds unevolved stars with A(Li)=2.58 and 2.51 dex, no rotation or chromospheric activity, ruling out in-situ production and planet engulfment and pointing to companion interaction scenarios.
AI.motivation: Li-rich stars are rare (only 16 known in GCs, spanning MS turnoff to RGB), and their origin remains debated. GCs offer a controlled environment to discriminate among proposed Li-enrichment mechanisms, motivating characterization of newly found Li-rich members.
AI.method: High-resolution UVES spectra analyzed with standard 1D LTE model-atmosphere abundance analysis; projected rotational velocity measured and chromospheric activity searched; abundances of 24 species (Li, C, N, O, Na, Mg, Al, Si, S, K, Ca, Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Sr, Y, Zr, Ba, Nd) derived for stars 44606, 58195, and 37934.
AI.result: A(Li)=2.58 dex (44606) and 2.51 dex (58195), significantly above the normal dwarf Li distribution in M4; A(Li)=3.01 dex for 37934, consistent with prior work. No detectable rotational broadening or chromospheric activity in any target; detailed abundances obtained for 24 species.
AI.conclusion: The unevolved nature of the Li-rich stars excludes in-situ Li production; planet engulfment is very unlikely in GCs and no present-day rotation/activity is seen. By exclusion, companion-interaction scenarios (dynamical interactions, mass transfer, mergers) are the most plausible remaining channels, though no companion has yet been detected.
